nodes.text: Korean barbecue
Dinner that night is Korean Barbecue. The restaurant looks like something out of a movie. Perhaps it is.

There is a very good likelihood of that. The production value is top notch the cast is gorgeous. Andy looks around the table at the nerdherd, pretty despite the grunge of vulgar educational excess and the resultant exhaustion.

They order like pros and the table is full of good uncooked food and kimchees of variety. They cook their meal in the communal center over a hotpot. Spencer and Jessie devour, absolutely devour like this is their first meal in weeks.

Andy wants to savor but must keep up because they inhale and the first round of dishes gone stuffed into gut and already undergoing physical transformation becoming liquid paste necessity for the hot young bodies.

Jessie leans into Spencer spent, they exhaust and expand and collapse cozy sexual into the other in tiny booth in a matter of minutes no conversation they are too far gone groggy elastic rubber band neck and shoulder and spine.

When they get back, Janessa walks Andy into the strange tall building fully lit alive and never sleeping, tallest on campus. They enter from the underground instead of aboveground. Tunnels network all the other underground entranceways.

People ride bikes along the long subterranean corridors, skateboard press off walls, find center handles to grind, feel them coming half a mile off, moto-scooter on through, graffiti that shit all up with whatever ink on hand.
That's one of the unwritten rules of Caltech. Write on everything, it's okay, feel free. If it's liked, your words and pictures will live in that spot for years.
If it's crap, it'll be the canvas for something far more worthy, the masterpiece of tomorrow's miscreant dreamer defiler.

Andy and Janessa pass rooms with radiation warning signs on doors, security checkpoints, clean rooms visible behind reinforced glass, people in lab coats, kids wearing 3D glasses playing racquetball in an empty room lit with red and blue Chinese lanterns.

On the ride back, Janessa told Andy about the psychophysics experiments she did. Says she knows some kids who are doing CAT scan sleeping experiments now and they're paying good money for every night they get you to participate. All the experiments are in the new building, Moore, in the Koch lab.
The hallways leading to the lab are lined by long empty aquariums once housing intricate families of electric eels.

For these experiments they're recruiting video game players figuring it'd be so much easier to train stimulation junkies to quickly respond to the computer prompts and visual stimuli. Video game generation deadheads see what makes them go batshit insane.
Caltech was where so much of the early LSD shit gave way exploded became. This is the same only different they say. The voices of intellect and reason and experimentation.
Janessa doesn't want to give it all away.

The room is in the basement's basement and a deathly heavy black curtain is pulled around the computer, a spanky Sun or something networked with slick handwritten Linux so the researcher can watch real time from the next room.
The chair is intentionally uncomfortable to discourage nodding off in the warm and darkened room.

The sleep study room is a small office with two beds. It has a homey feel, there are little touches that put Andy immediately at ease. A Kermit doll sits on top a computer monitor his eyes painted bloodshot red holding a real joint in his green felt hand.

A girl with black hair, bleached blue highlights says hello, immediately recognizing Janessa. They hug make excited to see you sounds catch-up quickly on the spot. Andy stands there unnoticed looking around.
There are movie posters on the walls. Altered States with William Hurt, the David Lynch film Lost Highway. There is a bookshelf between two beds, stacked full of good reads.
Jacques Deridan. Martin Heidegger. Wittgenstein.
The Corrections. Vollman. Richard Powers.
A portable CD player occupies part of one shelf.
The spines are cracked white from reading, read and reread.
